Thermal management is critical for high-frequency plasma operation. Continuous monitoring of transistor temperature and active cooling are essential to ensure long-term reliability. 2. Electrical insulation strategies must balance protection with charge dissipation. Redundant insulation layers can inadvertently store charge, increasing the risk of localized breakdown. 3. Data integrity requires robust EMI mitigation. Shielded cables, short signal paths, and isolated grounds are necessary for accurate diagnostics and sensor reliability when using pulsed plasmas with rapid current rise. The AJAX 2802’s ICC successfully adjusted to reformed-fuel combustion, demonstrating that modern engine-control algorithms can accommodate plasma-assisted operation with minimal tuning. 5. Incremental validation is effective. Progressing from bench to facility to engine testing provided clear performance verification at each stage while minimizing risk. These lessons have already informed subsequent reformer design improvements, including enhanced electrical connectors, simplified cooling manifolds, and streamlined diagnostic interfaces for future prototype iterations. 4.4 Summary of Outcomes All major technical challenges identified during the project were resolved without impact on schedule or deliverable completion. The resulting plasma reformer and pulse-power system operated reliably during high-flow and engine-scale tests, confirming the durability of the final configuration. The intellectual property developed under this project provides a clear pathway for commercialization and further research collaborations. The experience gained in overcoming electrical, thermal, and analytical challenges has strengthened the engineering framework for future plasma-based methane mitigation technologies and established a robust foundation for scale-up and field demonstration activities. SECTION 5 — Programmatic Impact, Conclusions, and Public Executive Summary 5.1 Alignment with DOE Program Objectives The work performed under Award DE-FE0032301 directly supported the U.S. Department of Energy’s objective to reduce methane leaks from natural gas infrastructure through innovative, energy-efficient technologies. The project aligned with the objectives of the DOE Office of Fossil Energy and Carbon Management’s objectives to reduce methane slip from existing natural-gas compression and power- generation assets. The plasma-based fuel reformer developed and demonstrated in this program addresses methane leaks by enabling on-demand production of hydrogen and reactive hydrocarbons directly within the engine fuel line. This eliminates the need for external hydrogen infrastructure while improving combustion completeness and reducing unburned methane in the exhaust. Measurable leak reductions of up to 27 percent in high-speed operation and 1–2 percent in the pre-chambers of large-bore stationary engines were achieved while consuming less than 0.3 percent of engine output power.
